one_liner: Rust wc clone with SIMD line and UTF-8 character counting; 1.5-70x faster than FreeBSD 12 wc and GNU wc 8.30 in 2019.
what_it_does: A command-line replacement for wc that counts lines, words, bytes, UTF-8 characters (-m) and the longest line (-L), with GNU-style --files-from/--files0-from and an optional --threads=N that counts several files in parallel. Output uses BSD-style fixed-width padding. The repo also builds as a small library (cw::count::Strategy and Counter), but that API is undocumented and unpublished beyond crates.io 0.7.0.
how_it_is_fast: At startup it picks the cheapest of seven specialised counting loops that covers the requested flags: -c uses stat() on regular files, -l uses bytecount::count (Joshua Landau's 'hyperscreamingcount' SWAR/SSE2/AVX2 byte counting), -m uses bytecount::num_chars (counts bytes that are not UTF-8 continuation bytes, no decoding), -lL scans with memchr, and only -mw-style combinations fall back to a bstr chars() loop. Files are opened with posix_fadvise(SEQUENTIAL) and read in 32 KiB blocks, and --threads hands whole files to a scoped worker pool. The wc baselines run one general loop for every flag combination (FreeBSD 12 wc does a scalar byte loop for -l and calls mbrtowc per character for -m; GNU 8.30 wc -L computes tab-expanded display width with wcwidth).
when_to_use: Counting lines (-l) or UTF-8 code points (-m) of large, well-formed UTF-8 files where a SIMD byte count is all you need.
Totalling many files at once on a multi-core box via --threads or --files0-from (the README's 12-thread xargs run was 11.55x faster than FreeBSD wc).
BSD systems where the system wc runs a scalar byte loop and GNU wc is held back by a weak libc memchr.
Scripts that only need -l, -c or -m and do not depend on locale-specific word or display-width rules.
when_not_to_use: Anything that relies on -L: the -lL fast path is buggy (see gotchas), and even when correct it reports bytes or characters, not GNU's tab-expanded display width.
Non-UTF-8 locales or legacy encodings: cw ignores the locale entirely; -m assumes UTF-8 and words without -m split on ASCII whitespace only (no vertical tab, no Unicode spaces).
Modern Linux with GNU coreutils 9.x for plain -l: coreutils 9.0 added an AVX2 newline counter (src/wc_avx2.c), so the 2019 -l ratios no longer describe that comparison.
Scripts parsing GNU wc output: cw always pads fields to 7 columns BSD-style (issues #4 and #8) and treats '-' as a file name rather than stdin.
Projects needing a maintained tool: last commit March 2021, open PR #6 and issues #5, #7, #8 unanswered, and the CHANGELOG's 0.8.0 was never tagged or published.

integration.form: crate (binary; also exposes an undocumented library)
integration.dependencies: bytecount 0.6, memchr 2, bstr 0.2, structopt 0.3 (clap 2), crossbeam-channel 0.5, crossbeam-utils 0.8, libc 0.2; winapi on Windows
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2018 edition; minimum rustc not documented (bytecount 0.6 needs Rust 1.32+); issue #7 shows a 2025 rustc builds it with one unexpected_cfgs warning
integration.platforms: Unix (posix_fadvise, F_RDAHEAD on macOS, SIGINFO on BSD/macOS and SIGUSR1 everywhere) and Windows (FILE_FLAG_SEQUENTIAL_SCAN); SIMD only via bytecount runtime-dispatch-simd (SSE2/AVX2 on x86) or nightly-only generic-simd, scalar elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: Single process CLI; --threads uses scoped threads with an atomic work index and prints results in input order; library thread safety not documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same core flags as wc (-c -l -w -m -L) plus GNU --files-from/--files0-from, but no locale support, -m and -c override each other instead of printing both, -L counts bytes or characters (FreeBSD semantics, not GNU display width), '-' is not stdin, and output padding is fixed-width

gotchas: Correctness bug in the -lL fast path (LinesLongest in src/count.rs, unchanged since the benchmarked v0.5.0): the line-length carry is overwritten instead of added when a 32 KiB read holds no newline, the first line of each file is counted one byte short, and a file whose first byte is a newline underflows usize (debug builds panic; release builds report 18446744073709551615). A Python transcription of the closure reports 47,231 for an 80,000-byte line and 4 instead of 5 for 'moooo\nfoo\n'. The README's -lL timings (1.73x and 15.07x) were taken on this code and its output was never shown.
Every -L path (-lL, -mlL, -wL, -mwL) ignores a final line without a trailing newline; GNU wc 8.30 counts it (its loop updates linelength after the read loop). FreeBSD 12 wc also skips it.

The 15.07x '-lL vs gwc' and 3.88x/18.95x '-mlL vs gwc' rows compare different work: GNU wc -L computes display width (tabs to every 8th column, wcwidth per character via mbrtowc), while cw and FreeBSD wc count bytes or characters. The 70-124x -m rows compare bytecount's continuation-byte count, which does no validation, against wc's per-character mbrtowc loop; on invalid UTF-8 the counts differ (FreeBSD counts each bad byte as a character and warns, cw counts stray continuation bytes as zero). The locale used for the runs and the content of test-utf-8.html are not stated.

SIGUSR1 is hooked on every Unix: sending it prints progress to stderr instead of terminating the process. The repo's CHANGELOG lists a 0.8.0 (posix_fadvise, threading tweaks) that was never tagged or published, so 'cargo install cw' gives 0.7.0 from July 2019.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick cw over wz (the other Rust wc) when you need -L, --files0-from or multi-file --threads on a BSD system; prefer wz for numbers against a current GNU wc on Linux. hwc and the Haskell and APL wc projects are demonstrations rather than maintained tools, so cw is the more practical drop-in of this group despite being unmaintained.
verified_claims_summary: In January 2019 the author ran hyperfine on FreeBSD 12 on a 2.1 GHz Westmere Xeon, timing cw 0.4-0.5 (built with runtime-dispatch-simd) against FreeBSD's base wc and GNU coreutils 8.30 wc on a 341 MB Dickens XML file: -l 3.44x and 4.17x faster, default counts 1.45x and 2.05x, -m 70x and 30x, and about 1.6x/2.4x single-threaded on a many-file run (derived from page data; 11.55x/17.31x with 12 threads). No rustc version, wc build flags, locale or benchmark script is given, and gwc's -L rows measure GNU's display-width semantics rather than the byte count cw computes.
status_note: Abandoned since March 2021 (crates.io 0.7.0 from 2019, 14k downloads) but MIT-licensed, about 850 lines of Rust and still builds on a 2025 toolchain; fine for -l, -c and -m on UTF-8 files, but do not trust its -L output: the -lL fast path has an unfixed carry and off-by-one bug.
